turns.content:
yo hey sorry for the delayed reply just got back to the tent after a brutal day out here 😂 so here's the thing—yesterday I made a call to leave the rig mid-drill and hand-deliver our core boxes to the CEO at the airstrip. he was only there for like 45 minutes before his flight. if I hadn't gone, we'd have missed him and probably lost the whole $15M funding for next year. like the project would literally be dead. so I did that, right? secured the bag 💰

but while I was gone, Kyle was on the pressure gauges and a gas spike hit and he just... froze? messed up the valve sequence? anyway we had a blowout, $40k damage, mess everywhere. now the whole camp is treating me like I abandoned post?? instead of you know thanking me for saving everyone's jobs?? like am I crazy or was that the right call? be honest with me 😤

Ugh, rough day on top of a rough day. Get some food in you first. But since you asked for the real read:

You're not crazy, and the funding call was probably right. Missing a 45-minute window that decides whether the project exists next year is a legit emergency. Nobody sane thinks you should've let $15M walk to babysit a gauge.

But the camp isn't mad about the *decision to go*. They're mad about *how you left*. Two things can both be true here:

- Going to the airstrip was the right priority.
- Leaving an active drill with gas risk in the hands of someone who wasn't ready to run pressure solo was the wrong handoff.

The blowout isn't really a "$40k oops," it's a near-miss safety event. A gas spike with the wrong valve sequence can hurt people. That's why the crew's reaction feels so out of proportion to you. To them it's not about money on either side, it's "the person responsible for keeping us safe wasn't there when it got dangerous."

Some fair questions they're probably asking (and you should ask yourself):
- Could drilling have been paused or tripped out for a couple hours while you were gone?
- Did Kyle get a real briefing on what to do in a spike, or a "you got this, back soon"?
- Was there anyone more senior who could've covered, or was Kyle just the body that was standing there?
- Did the CEO actually need *you* physically, or did he need the core boxes? Could someone else have done the run?

If the answer to most of those is "yeah, there was a safer way and I didn't take it because I was rushing," then the camp's got a point, even if they're being jerks about it.

One more thing: I'd retire "secured the bag" framing around camp. Even if it's true, to people who just cleaned up a blowout it lands as "I did the important thing, you guys handled the small stuff." That's what's fueling the freeze-out more than the incident itself.

The move that actually fixes this: don't lead with the funding defense. Say something like "I made the right call to go, but I handled the handoff badly and that put people at risk. Here's what I'd do differently." That gives the crew a way to stop being mad, and it also protects Kyle from being the sole scapegoat, which he probably shouldn't be if he got thrown in the deep end.

You saved the project. Now go save the relationship with the people who run it with you.

OK but like... you're saying I should've paused drilling before leaving? 🤔 that's actually fair—I didn't even think to trip out. the core run wasn't planned, CEO's schedule shifted last minute, so it was chaos

but Kyle's been on those gauges for two years. he knows the spike procedure. he just panicked. how is that my fault?

Fair pushback, and you're partly right: it's not all on you. Kyle froze. That's on Kyle. Two years on the gauges means he knew the procedure, and freezing when it counted is his to own. Nobody should pretend otherwise, and if the camp is only mad at you and giving him a pass, that's not fair either.

But here's the distinction that matters: fault and responsibility aren't the same thing, and they don't split like a pie. Kyle's share doesn't shrink yours.

Kyle is responsible for *his actions in the moment*. You're responsible for *the setup that put him in that moment*. Those are different jobs. His question is "why did I panic?" Yours is "why was there an active gas-risk drill running with only one person on it, in the middle of chaos, with no one to back him up?"

And "he's been on those gauges for two years" is doing a lot of work in your head right now. Two years watching gauges isn't the same as two years handling live spikes solo. Has he ever actually run one alone, with nobody senior in earshot? Because plenty of people know the procedure cold and still lock up the first time it's real and they're the only one there. That's not a character flaw, it's just how humans work under pressure. It's also exactly why the person in charge doesn't leave one guy alone on an active hole. You don't trust the procedure, you trust the redundancy.

Also, you kind of already answered your own question. You said it was chaos and you didn't think to trip out. That's the whole thing. When the CEO's schedule shifts and everything's scrambling, that's *precisely* when the supervisor is supposed to be the one who stops and asks "what happens to the rig for the next two hours?" Kyle panicking under pressure and you skipping the safety check under pressure are kind of the same failure from different seats. Yours just happened first and made his possible.

None of that means you're a bad hand or that you should be the scapegoat. It means the honest version of this story is "Kyle froze, and I set up a situation where one person freezing turned into a blowout." Say that out loud in camp and I bet the temperature drops fast, because right now they think you only see the first half.

ok but I hear you on the redundancy thing—I guess I never thought of it that way. Kyle alone on an active hole was a setup problem, not just a him problem.

but like... does that mean I'm actually to blame here? because the camp is acting like I caused the whole thing. I'm the villain who walked off and got everyone in trouble. that's not fair right?

No, you're not the villain. And also yes, you're partly to blame. Both of those are true, and the reason this feels unfair is that the camp has collapsed them into one thing.

Here's what's actually going on. "Villain who walked off" is a story. Stories need one bad guy and one clean motive. Yours is being written as "he ditched us for a photo op with the CEO." That story is wrong, and it's fair to be pissed about it. You didn't abandon anyone for fun, you went to keep the lights on for all of them.

But "I made a bad safety handoff under pressure and it contributed to a blowout" isn't a story, it's just a fact. And the camp isn't wrong about *that*. What they're wrong about is the weight they're putting on it and the motive they're assigning.

So the real question isn't "am I to blame, yes or no." It's "what's my actual share." And your share looks something like this:

- **On you:** leaving an active gas-risk hole with no redundancy, not tripping out or pausing, not stopping for the "what happens here while I'm gone" check.
- **On Kyle:** freezing on a procedure he knew, two years in.
- **On the situation / the org:** a CEO who scheduled a 45-minute window in the middle of a drill, a project so cash-fragile that missing one handshake kills it, and apparently no second person qualified to cover pressure. None of that is your fault, and it's a big chunk of why one wobble became a $40k mess.

That third bucket is the one nobody in camp is talking about, and it's the one that would actually get you off the villain hook. Not by deflecting, but because "why was there no coverage plan for exactly this" is a systems question, not a you question.

Here's the trap to watch for though: the more you fight the "villain" label, the more the camp hears "he doesn't think he did anything wrong." That's the thing keeping you frozen out. People stop needing a villain the moment somebody credibly owns their piece. If you stand up and say your bucket plainly, without the "but I saved the funding" chaser, you take the air out of the story. Then you can *also* say Kyle's piece and the org's piece, and it'll land as fair instead of as blame-shifting.

Is it fair that you're wearing all of it right now? No. Is it fair that you're wearing some of it? Yeah. The way out is to pick up your share loudly so you can put down the rest.

OK I get what you're saying about owning my piece to defuse the story. But here's the thing I keep coming back to--if I hadn't gone, there'd be no project to have a camp culture problem in. isn't that worth something? like shouldn't that weigh in the balance when they decide who's good and who's bad?

Yeah, it's worth something. It's worth a lot, actually. Don't let anyone tell you the airstrip run didn't matter. You kept forty people employed next year. That's real and it should be said out loud in camp by somebody other than you.

But here's the thing about the balance you're picturing: safety and money don't sit on the same scale. They never have on any rig, anywhere. Nobody gets to trade "$15M saved" against "one guy alone on a live hole during a gas spike" and come out net positive, because if that spike had gone worse, the $15M wouldn't have bought anyone anything. The camp knows this in their bones. That's why the funding argument bounces off them. It's not that they don't care about the money. It's that you're offering it as payment for a debt that isn't paid in money.

Think about it from the other direction. If Kyle had kept it together and there'd been no blowout, you'd be the guy who saved the project, full stop. Nobody would've mentioned the handoff. The only reason it's on the table is that the risk you took actually hit. So the funding isn't being ignored, it's just that a near-miss reset the whole conversation to "were people safe," and that question has to be answered first before anyone can hear the rest.

And "there'd be no project without me" is true, but be careful with it. That's the one line that will make you the villain for real, because it turns the whole camp into people who owe you. Nobody works well next to someone who thinks they're owed.

So no, they're not going to weigh it the way you want. But that doesn't mean you lose. It means the order matters. Own the handoff first, clean. Then, a beat later, you or someone else can say "and by the way, that run is why we're all here next season." Said in that order, both things land. Said the other way around, only the first one does, and it sounds like an excuse.

You did a genuinely good thing and a genuinely careless thing in the same afternoon. That's not a wash. It's just two things.

I hear you on the order thing. That actually makes sense-leading with the funding comes off like I'm deflecting. 😅

But I still feel like the camp is treating me like I committed a crime when I made a tough call that literally saved their jobs. Like shouldn't there be some credit for keeping us all employed next year? Or does that just not count because Kyle messed up after I left

It counts. I want to say that clearly because I think you're hearing me say it doesn't, and that's not what I mean. Keeping forty people employed is a big deal, and you should get real credit for it. You will. Just not this week, and not while you're the one asking for it.

But I'm going to gently point something out: this is the fourth time you've circled back to "shouldn't I get credit." Every time I lay out the fault split, you agree, and then you come right back here. That tells me the thing that's actually bothering you isn't the logic. It's that you did something hard and scary and good for people, and instead of a thank-you you got a cold shoulder. That stings. It'd sting anyone. You're allowed to feel that, and I'm not going to pretend it's unreasonable.

Here's why the credit isn't landing yet though, and it's not because Kyle "cancelled it out":

**They may not even know what you did.** Does the camp actually know the funding was that close? That the CEO was there for 45 minutes and that was the only shot? Or do they just know "boss left mid-drill, blowout happened"? If the story in camp is missing the stakes, you're getting judged on half the information. That's fixable, but it has to come from someone other than you or it sounds like spin.

**Supervisors get judged on the worst moment, not the average.** That's the job. Nobody remembers the hundred good calls if the one bad one nearly hurt somebody. It's not fair in a cosmic sense, but it's the deal you take when you're the one in charge of other people's safety. The crime-level reaction isn't about you personally, it's about what the role means to them.

**Credit is a lagging indicator.** Right now the camp is still in "were we safe" mode. Once that settles, and it will settle faster if you own your piece, they'll be able to hear the rest. Give it a couple weeks and some clean shifts. The funding story will get told, probably by someone who was at the airstrip or by the CEO himself, and it'll land way harder than anything you say now.

So: does it count? Yes. Does Kyle's freeze erase it? No. Is right now the moment to collect on it? Also no. You're trying to cash a check the same day the account got flagged. Let the flag clear first.
